passage_title: Soil Fungi and the Growth of Orvala Seedlings
passage:
Many plants form partnerships with soil fungi whose threads grow into the plant's roots. The fungus receives sugars from the plant, and the plant may receive water and mineral nutrients gathered by the fungal threads. Whether the plant gains or loses from the partnership can depend on growing conditions.

Botanists studied Orvala, a small herb, and three strains of a root-colonizing soil fungus, labeled K1, K2, and K3. In every trial, 12 Orvala seedlings were planted one per pot in heat-sterilized soil (soil heated to kill any fungi already present). Seedlings were either left uninoculated or inoculated with one fungal strain at planting. After 30 days, the botanists measured the percent of each plant's total root length that was colonized by fungal threads and the plant's shoot dry mass (the mass of its stems and leaves after drying). Table 1 gives the average values for each trial.

Experiment 1
Seedlings were left uninoculated or were inoculated with K1, K2, or K3. All were grown at a soil moisture of 25% (water as a percent of soil mass) with no Compound M added.

Experiment 2
Seedlings were left uninoculated or were inoculated with K2 and were grown at soil moistures of 10%, 40%, and 55% with no Compound M added. (The 25% results for these two conditions are those of Experiment 1.)

Experiment 3
Compound M, an unnamed synthetic chemical, was mixed into the soil at 5 or 20 mg per kg of soil. Seedlings were left uninoculated or were inoculated with K2 and were grown at a soil moisture of 25%. (The 0 mg/kg results for these two conditions are those of Experiment 1.)

graphic.caption: Table 1. Root colonization and shoot dry mass of Orvala seedlings after 30 days

prompt: Based on Experiments 1 and 2, at which soil moisture was the shoot dry mass of uninoculated seedlings greatest, and at which soil moisture was the shoot dry mass of K2-inoculated seedlings greatest?
explanation: With no Compound M, uninoculated shoot mass was 88 mg (10%), 142 mg (25%), 176 mg (40%), and 151 mg (55%), so it peaked at 40%. K2 shoot mass was 131, 208, 197, and 149 mg at the same moistures, so it peaked at 25%.
subskill: locate maxima in two series across two experiments
consistency_check: Uninoculated seedlings in sterilized soil show 0% colonization in every row; all colonization values are 0-100%; the 25%/0 mg/kg rows are reused, not repeated, as the passage states; every benefit used by Q2/Q6 recomputed: 10% 131-88=43, 25% 208-142=66, 40% 197-176=21, 55% 149-151=-2, M5 236-150=86, M20 171-139=32. No named law generates any cell (optimum in moisture, reversal of K2 benefit at 55% and 20 mg/kg).

passage_title: Gas Release from Compound L with Three Catalysts
passage:
When a solid catalyst powder is stirred into a water solution of Compound L, an unnamed substance, L breaks down and releases a gas. Without a catalyst, less than 1 mL of gas forms in 30 minutes at any of the temperatures used below.

In each trial, chemists placed 50.0 mL of the same L solution in a flask held at a set temperature, stirred in a catalyst powder, and collected the gas released. They recorded the volume of gas released in the first 5 minutes and the total volume released by the time gas stopped forming. All gas volumes were measured after the gas had been brought to 25 °C and 1 atm. The chemists call 0.20 g of catalyst at 30 °C the standard conditions.

Experiment 1
Three unnamed catalysts, R, S, and T, were each tested under the standard conditions.

Experiment 2
0.20 g of Catalyst S was tested at 20, 30, 40, 50, and 60 °C.

Experiment 3
Catalyst S was tested at 30 °C with 0.05, 0.10, 0.20, and 0.40 g of catalyst.

graphic.caption: Table 1. Gas released from 50.0 mL of Compound L solution (volumes at 25 °C and 1 atm)

prompt: In Experiment 2, between which two consecutive temperatures did the gas volume released in the first 5 minutes change by the greatest amount (whether an increase or a decrease)?
explanation: The 5-minute volumes were 31, 58, 77, 70, and 41 mL at 20-60 °C. The changes are +27, +19, -7, and -29 mL, so the largest change, 29 mL, was between 50 °C and 60 °C.
subskill: compare successive differences
consistency_check: Same 50.0 mL of L in every trial, so no total exceeds 96 mL; every 5-min volume is below its total; volumes are corrected to 25 C and 1 atm so totals at different temperatures are comparable; the standard trial (S, 0.20 g, 30 C) reads 58/96 in all three experiments; uncatalyzed release <1 mL, so the 60 C total of 81 mL is the catalyst stopping early, not a stoichiometry change. Optimum at 40 C and plateau in mass are invented, not Arrhenius or a rate law.

passage_title: Floodplain Deposits in a Laboratory Channel
passage:
When a river floods, water spreads over its floodplain, slows down, and drops some of the sediment (mud and sand grains) it carries. Plants on a floodplain can change how much sediment settles and what size of grains settle.

Geologists studying the floodplain of the Merrin River built a 12 m long laboratory channel with a raised shelf along one side to represent the floodplain. Rigid plastic rods 5 mm wide stood upright on the shelf to represent plant stems. In each trial, water carrying the same concentration of Merrin River sediment (2.0 g per liter) flowed through the channel and across the shelf. The flow speed was measured in the main channel just upstream of the shelf. After each trial, the geologists measured the average thickness of the deposit left on the shelf and its median grain size (half of the deposited grains, by mass, were smaller than this size).

Experiment 1
The shelf held 0, 100, 400, or 1,600 rods per square meter. Water flowed at 0.30 m/s for 6 hours.

Experiment 2
The shelf held 400 rods per square meter. Water flowed for 6 hours at 0.15, 0.30, 0.45, or 0.60 m/s.

Experiment 3
The shelf held 400 rods per square meter. Water flowed at 0.30 m/s for 2, 6, 12, or 24 hours.

graphic.caption: Table 1. Shelf deposits in the laboratory channel

prompt: In which experiment(s) did the deposit thickness increase every time the quantity being varied was increased?
explanation: Experiment 1 thickness rose from 1.2 to 3.8 to 5.1 mm but fell to 2.0 mm at 1,600 rods/m². Experiment 2 rose from 2.2 to 5.1 mm, then fell to 4.4 and 1.6 mm. Experiment 3 rose every time: 1.9, 5.1, 7.6, 8.3 mm.
subskill: identify monotonic trends
consistency_check: The standard trial (400 rods, 0.30 m/s, 6 h) reads 5.1 mm / 66 um in all three experiments; thickness grows with duration but each later hour adds less (0.95, 0.80, 0.42, 0.06 mm/h), as a fixed sediment supply allows; faster flow gives coarser grains at every step (22, 66, 95, 118); the 1,600-rod deposit (2.0 mm, 104 um) lies between the 0.45 and 0.60 m/s deposits on BOTH measures, so Q6's inference is unique. Thickness optimum and the coarse dense-rod deposit follow no named law.

passage_title: The Two Layers of Lake Varn
passage:
Lake Varn is 40 m deep and lies in a closed mountain basin. One river, the Ostle, flows into the lake; no river flows out. Water leaves the lake by evaporation and by seepage through sandy ground at the southern shore. The lake has a northern basin and a southern basin, 2 km apart, each 40 m deep.

The lake water is divided into two layers that never mix with each other. The top layer, from the surface to 18 m, is nearly fresh (salinity 0.4 g/kg, meaning 0.4 g of dissolved salts per kilogram of water) and is mixed by wind every winter. Below 18 m, salinity rises steeply, and the bottom layer, from 22 m down to the floor, has a salinity of 14 g/kg and contains no dissolved oxygen. In Ostle River water, chloride makes up about 20% of the dissolved negative ions and sulfate about 70%. Two scientists explain the origin of the bottom layer.

Scientist 1
The bottom layer is fed by springs. A fault (a crack in the rock) crosses the floor of the northern basin. Groundwater rising along the fault dissolves a buried salt bed and enters the lake as springs whose water has a salinity of about 30 g/kg; chloride makes up more than 90% of its negative ions. Because the spring water is denser than lake water, it spreads along the lake floor, mixing with some lake water, and almost all of the bottom layer's dissolved salt comes from the springs. Salt slowly diffuses upward out of the bottom layer, but the springs replace it as fast as it is lost, so the bottom layer's salinity and the depth of its top, 22 m, stay constant. Salinity 1 m above the floor should be a few tenths of a g/kg higher in the northern basin, near the springs, than in the southern basin. The springs, and the layering, began when the fault became active at least 600 years ago.

Scientist 2
The bottom layer is left over from a drought. About 900 years ago, a long drought lowered the lake until it was only 20 m deep. Evaporation concentrated the salts brought in by the Ostle River until the remaining water had a salinity of about 25 g/kg, without changing the proportions of the dissolved ions. When wetter conditions returned, fresh river water refilled the lake to 40 m and floated on top of the dense brine, which remained as the bottom 20 m of the lake. No salt has entered the bottom layer since. Salt slowly diffuses upward out of the bottom layer, and the winter mixing of the top layer wears away the top of the bottom layer, so the bottom layer's salinity has been falling and its top has moved down by about 2 m since the drought. Because the brine formed throughout the lake at once, salinity at any given depth in the bottom layer should be the same in both basins.

Lake Varn is 40 m deep and lies in a closed mountain basin. One river, the Ostle, flows into the lake; no river flows out. Water leaves the lake by evaporation and by seepage through sandy ground at the southern shore. The lake has a northern basin and a southern basin, 2 km apart, each 40 m deep.

The lake water is divided into two layers that never mix with each other. The top layer, from the surface to 18 m, is nearly fresh (salinity 0.4 g/kg, meaning 0.4 g of dissolved salts per kilogram of water) and is mixed by wind every winter. Below 18 m, salinity rises steeply, and the bottom layer, from 22 m down to the floor, has a salinity of 14 g/kg and contains no dissolved oxygen. In Ostle River water, chloride makes up about 20% of the dissolved negative ions and sulfate about 70%. Two scientists explain the origin of the bottom layer.

Scientist 1
The bottom layer is fed by springs. A fault (a crack in the rock) crosses the floor of the northern basin. Groundwater rising along the fault dissolves a buried salt bed and enters the lake as springs whose water has a salinity of about 30 g/kg; chloride makes up more than 90% of its negative ions. Because the spring water is denser than lake water, it spreads along the lake floor, mixing with some lake water, and almost all of the bottom layer's dissolved salt comes from the springs. Salt slowly diffuses upward out of the bottom layer, but the springs replace it as fast as it is lost, so the bottom layer's salinity and the depth of its top, 22 m, stay constant. Salinity 1 m above the floor should be a few tenths of a g/kg higher in the northern basin, near the springs, than in the southern basin. The springs, and the layering, began when the fault became active at least 600 years ago.

Scientist 2
The bottom layer is left over from a drought. About 900 years ago, a long drought lowered the lake until it was only 20 m deep. Evaporation concentrated the salts brought in by the Ostle River until the remaining water had a salinity of about 25 g/kg, without changing the proportions of the dissolved ions. When wetter conditions returned, fresh river water refilled the lake to 40 m and floated on top of the dense brine, which remained as the bottom 20 m of the lake. No salt has entered the bottom layer since. Salt slowly diffuses upward out of the bottom layer, and the winter mixing of the top layer wears away the top of the bottom layer, so the bottom layer's salinity has been falling and its top has moved down by about 2 m since the drought. Because the brine formed throughout the lake at once, salinity at any given depth in the bottom layer should be the same in both basins.

explanation: Scientist 2 dates the drought, and so the bottom layer, to about 900 years ago. Scientist 1 says the layering began at least 600 years ago, and 900 years is at least 600 years, so the finding fits both views.

passage_title: Why Do Lagoon Lacecorals Turn Pale?
passage:
Orrasea is a colonial animal of tropical lagoons that builds branching limestone skeletons. Its living outer tissue contains velarin, a purple pigment the animal makes itself. A colony is called pale when it has less than 10% of its normal amount of velarin. Pale colonies survive and can regain their color. In Tessan Lagoon, which is 1 to 6 m deep and has a river entering along its west shore, the percent of Orrasea colonies that were pale each September is shown in Figure 1. Three scientists explain the paling.

Scientist 1
Paling is caused by ultraviolet (UV) light, which breaks velarin down faster than a colony can replace it. Since 2017 the lagoon water has become clearer, and the UV light reaching 2 m depth has roughly doubled. UV light is absorbed as it passes down through the water, so colonies deeper than 4 m do not pale, and on a shallower colony the upward-facing surfaces of the branches pale first while the shaded undersides stay purple. A pale colony moved to 5 m depth regains full color in about 3 weeks.

Scientist 2
Paling is caused by low salinity. After heavy rains, river water spreads across the lagoon as a fresh layer about 2 m thick that floats on the saltier lagoon water. When the salinity around a colony stays below 28 g/kg for more than 5 days, the colony stops making velarin, and the velarin it has is lost as its outer tissue is replaced. Paling appears within 2 weeks of a heavy rain, affects all surfaces of a colony evenly, and is greatest near the west shore; colonies deeper than 2 m, below the fresh layer, do not pale. A pale colony regains full color about 6 weeks after the salinity returns to normal.

Scientist 3
Paling is caused by Y-4, a bacterium that digests velarin. An infection begins at a single spot on a colony and spreads across the colony at about 1 cm per day, and it passes from colony to colony where branches touch. Y-4 grows faster in water warmer than 29 °C, so more colonies pale in warmer summers. Paling occurs at every depth in the lagoon, with no preference for upward-facing or downward-facing surfaces. Once Y-4 is cleared from a colony, the colony regains full color in about 6 weeks.

explanation: The percent fell from 9% in 2018 to 7% in 2019 and from 22% in 2021 to 15% in 2022. It rose in every other year-to-year step, including 2019 to 2020 (7% to 18%) and 2022 to 2023 (15% to 33%).

passage_title: Gas G in the Atmosphere of Kessa b
passage:
Kessa b is a rocky planet that orbits a small, cool star every 6.2 days and always keeps the same side facing the star. When the planet passes in front of the star (a transit), some starlight passes through the planet's atmosphere at its edge, or limb, and astronomers can measure which gases are present. The morning limb is the edge where the planet's rotation carries gas from the night side into daylight; the evening limb is the opposite edge.

During six transits, astronomers measured Gas G, an unnamed molecule, in Kessa b's atmosphere, along with how many strong flares (sudden outbursts that fling energetic particles outward) the star produced in the 5 days before each transit (Table 1). Starlight destroys G: about half of the G present at any time is gone 3 days later. Gas P is abundant in the atmosphere. Two scientists explain the changes in G.

Scientist 1
G forms when energetic particles from strong flares strike molecules of Gas P high in the atmosphere and break them apart. Each strong flare adds about 4 to 6 parts per million (ppm) of G within a day, and winds spread the new G evenly around the planet within hours, so G should be about equally abundant on the morning and evening limbs. Between flares, ordinary starlight breaks apart enough P to keep G at about 2 to 3 ppm. Kessa b's volcanoes, if any, are too weak to matter, so Gas S, a sulfur gas released by eruptions, should not be detected.

Scientist 2
G comes from volcanic eruptions. Eruptions vent large amounts of Gas P together with Gas S, and starlight breaks the new P apart into G within hours. Because the volcanic region lies near the morning limb, for about 2 days after an eruption G is at least twice as abundant on the morning limb as on the evening limb; after 3 to 4 days, winds have spread it evenly. Between eruptions, slow venting keeps G at about 2 to 3 ppm. Flares do not affect G; high G after flares at some transits is a coincidence.

prompt: According to Table 1, at which transit was G most unevenly divided between the two limbs, and how many strong flares had the star produced in the 5 days before that transit?
explanation: The morning-to-evening ratio was 3.2 at Transit 5, far from the values of 0.9 to 1.1 at the other transits, and Table 1 lists 0 strong flares before Transit 5.
